title: Quality assurance vs quality control
blurb: Differentiate quality assurance (process, confidence, prevention) from quality control (product, checking, detection), and explain why a project needs both.
question: A bank's app team says: 'We test every release thoroughly, so we don't need anyone auditing how we work.' Explain the difference between what the testers do and what an audit does, and why the project needs both.

teach.body: Quality ASSURANCE provides confidence that the project will satisfy the relevant quality standards, by checking that the agreed processes and standards are being followed and are working. It is process-focused, preventive and ideally independent of the delivery team. Quality CONTROL checks the outputs themselves through inspection, testing and measurement. It is product-focused and detective. Plain English: QA asks 'are we working in a way that will produce quality?'; QC asks 'is this output right?'

teach.h: QA versus QC at a glance

teach.caption: Both are planned in the quality management plan and work to the same agreed standards. They look at different things.

teach.body: QC on its own catches defects, but often late, and the same defects keep coming back because nobody fixes the way the work is done. QA on its own gives confidence the process is followed, but nobody confirms the actual outputs meet their criteria. Together: QA prevents defects by making the process sound; QC detects the ones that still get through and feeds that data back to QA. Prevention is generally cheaper than finding and fixing defects.

teach.loop: Fewer defects reach QC next time

teach.body: Meridian's testers test every release against its acceptance criteria: that's QC. Each quarter, an assurance reviewer from the PMO, independent of the team, checks that secure-coding standards, code reviews and the test process are actually being followed: that's QA. The review finds code reviews are skipped under deadline pressure, which explains why login defects keep reappearing in testing. The process is fixed, and login defects fall. The testers caught the symptom; assurance fixed the cause.

teach.h: Defects keep reaching customers: what does the audit say?
teach.caption: If a well-followed process still produces defects, more inspection only finds them: the process must change.

teach.h: QA and QC in linear and iterative life cycles

rows.label: QC
values: Inspections and tests at stage ends; acceptance
Testing within every time box; demos

rows.label: QA
values: Audits and health checks at stages and gates

teach.caption: A retrospective is the team improving its own process. Independent assurance still checks the method is being applied properly.

teach.text: The classic mix-up. AUDIT, process review, preventive, independent, confidence = QA. INSPECTION, testing, measurement, sampling, detective, defects = QC. Watch the word 'review': reviewing a deliverable (a design walkthrough) is QC; reviewing whether the process is followed is QA.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define QA: confidence that the project will meet quality standards, by checking processes are followed and effective (audits, reviews).
Define QC: checking outputs against acceptance criteria (inspection, testing, measurement, sampling).
Differentiate: process vs product, preventive vs detective, independent vs delivery team.
Explain why both: QC catches defects; QA prevents them recurring and gives the board confidence.
Apply to the scenario with one example of each.
QA = process, confidence, prevention, ideally independent (audits, health checks).
QC = product, checking, detection, delivery team (inspection, testing, measurement, sampling).
QC finds defects; QA uses the findings to fix their causes.
Process followed but defects persist: improve the process. Process not followed: improve adherence.
Reviewing a deliverable is QC; reviewing how work is done is QA.

summary: You can now differentiate quality assurance from quality control by focus, aim, timing and who does it, and classify activities such as audits and tests correctly. You can also explain why a project needs both, and how QC findings feed QA improvements.

A.q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of quality assurance?
options: To find defects in the finished outputs before handover
To give confidence the processes will deliver quality
To approve outputs on behalf of the project sponsor
To set the acceptance criteria for each deliverable
A.why: QA provides confidence that the project will satisfy the relevant quality standards, by checking that processes are followed and effective.

whyNot.0: Finding defects in outputs is quality control.
whyNot.2: Approving outputs is acceptance, by users, the sponsor or the product owner.
whyNot.3: Setting acceptance criteria is quality planning.

A.q: Which activity is an example of quality CONTROL rather than quality assurance?
options: An audit of whether teams follow the test procedure
A PMO health check of the project's quality processes
A review of how well the defect process is working
Testing a batch of finished parts against the spec
A.why: Testing finished parts against a specification checks the product itself: that is QC.

whyNot.0: Auditing whether a procedure is followed checks the process: QA.
whyNot.1: A health check of processes is an assurance activity.
whyNot.2: Reviewing how well a process works is QA, even when the process is about defects.

A.q: Which pair of words BEST describes quality assurance?
options: Preventive and process-focused
Detective and product-focused
Reactive and output-focused
Optional and delivery-team-led
A.why: QA aims to prevent defects by making sure the processes are sound and followed.

whyNot.1: Detective and product-focused describes quality control.
whyNot.2: Reacting to outputs is closer to QC, and QA is planned, not reactive.
whyNot.3: QA is planned in the quality management plan and ideally independent of the delivery team.

B.q: An audit finds teams are following the agreed processes correctly, yet defects keep reaching customers. What is the BEST response?
options: Add more inspection at the end and leave the process alone
Stop the audits, since they are showing that all is well
Improve the process itself, as following it isn't enough
Retrain the teams on the processes they already follow
B.why: If a process is followed correctly but still produces defects, the process itself is inadequate and must be improved.

whyNot.0: More inspection finds more defects but doesn't stop them being produced.
whyNot.1: The audit shows the process is followed, not that quality is good; defects prove otherwise.
whyNot.3: Teams already follow the process, so retraining won't fix a flawed process.

B.q: Why should quality assurance ideally be carried out by people independent of the delivery team?
options: Independent staff are cheaper than the delivery team
It gives an objective view, free from delivery pressure
The delivery team is not allowed to see quality records
Independent people are better at testing the outputs
B.why: Independence gives an objective, unbiased view of whether processes are followed, which is what gives the board real confidence.

whyNot.0: Cost isn't the reason; independent reviewers may cost more.
whyNot.2: Quality records are shared; the team needs them to improve.
whyNot.3: Testing outputs is QC, usually done by the delivery team or testers.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are quality assurance activities?
1. A process audit
2. Inspecting welds on a frame
3. Reviewing how well the testing process works
4. Sampling a batch of delivered goods
options: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: A process audit (1) and a review of the testing process (3) both examine processes: QA.

whyNot.1: Inspecting welds (2) checks the product: QC.
whyNot.2: Both inspecting welds (2) and sampling goods (4) check products: QC.
whyNot.3: Sampling delivered goods (4) checks products: QC.

C.q: A project's QC records show defect numbers falling steadily after the PMO changed the code review process. Which statement BEST explains this?
options: QC has replaced the need for any further QA activity
The acceptance criteria must have been made less strict
Testing has become less thorough since the change
A QA improvement prevented defects that QC would find
C.why: Improving the process (QA) prevents defects, so QC finds fewer. This is the two working together as intended.

whyNot.0: The fall came from a QA change, so QA is clearly still needed.
whyNot.1: Nothing suggests the criteria changed; the process did.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests testing changed; the improvement was upstream.

C.q: A project manager says: 'We test everything thoroughly, so we don't need quality assurance.' What is the flaw in this argument?
options: Testing is a QA activity, so QA is already happening
Thorough testing is only needed on iterative projects
Testing finds defects but doesn't prevent their causes
QA is a legal requirement on every UK project of any size
C.why: Testing is QC: it detects defects. Without QA, nobody checks or improves the processes that cause them, and there's no independent confidence.

whyNot.0: Testing is quality control, not quality assurance.
whyNot.1: Testing is needed in every life cycle.
whyNot.3: QA is good practice and governance, not a universal legal requirement.

C.q: On an iterative project, the team tests each feature within the time box, and an independent reviewer later checks the team applies its agreed method properly. Which is correct?
options: Both activities are quality control of the outputs
The testing is QC; the independent review is QA
The testing is QA; the independent review is QC
Both activities are quality assurance of processes
C.why: Testing features checks the product (QC). Reviewing whether the method is applied properly checks the process (QA).

whyNot.0: The reviewer examines the method, not the outputs, so that part is QA.
whyNot.2: This reverses them: testing is product-focused QC; a method review is QA.
whyNot.3: Testing features checks outputs, so that part is QC.

reteach.title: A restaurant kitchen
reteach.question: In a busy restaurant, the head chef tastes every plate before it leaves the pass, and the owner checks the kitchen's routines each month. Which is QA and which is QC?

blocks.h: Tasting the plate vs checking the kitchen
blocks.body: The head chef tasting each plate at the pass is quality control: checking the product before it reaches the customer, and sending it back if it's wrong. The owner checking that recipes are followed, fridge temperatures are logged and cleaning routines happen is quality assurance: making sure the way the kitchen works will produce good food every time. If the same dish keeps getting sent back, tasting harder won't fix it. Someone has to fix the recipe or the routine.

blocks.h: The pass versus the routine check

blocks.text: QC = taste the plate (product). QA = check the kitchen (process). You need both.

explain.body: Quality assurance provides confidence that the project will satisfy the relevant quality standards. It does this by evaluating performance and checking that the agreed processes and standards are being followed and are working.

test.q: Complete the statement: quality assurance provides ______ that the project will satisfy the relevant quality standards.
options: a guarantee
acceptance
confidence
approval
test.why: QA provides confidence, through checking processes, that the project will meet its quality standards.

whyNot.0: No activity can guarantee quality; QA gives confidence, not certainty.
whyNot.1: Acceptance of outputs comes from users or the sponsor after QC.
whyNot.3: Approval is a governance decision, not the purpose of QA.

explain.body: Quality control checks the outputs themselves against their criteria, using inspection, testing, measurement and sampling. It detects defects so they can be fixed before acceptance.

test.q: A food manufacturer checks a sample of pies from each batch for weight and temperature. This is:
options: quality control, as it checks the product
quality assurance, as it checks the process
quality planning, as it sets the standards
continuous improvement, as it fixes causes
test.why: Checking samples of the actual pies against criteria checks the product: QC.

whyNot.1: The pies are products, not a process, so this isn't QA.
whyNot.2: Planning sets the weight and temperature criteria; this is checking against them.
whyNot.3: Nothing here fixes causes; it detects whether the pies meet criteria.

explain.body: A quality audit is a systematic, ideally independent check that the agreed processes are being followed and are effective. It does not find defects in individual outputs: that's QC.

test.q: Which statement about quality audits is correct?
options: They find and fix defects in individual outputs
They replace the need for testing the outputs
They give the sponsor's approval to each output
They check that agreed processes are followed
test.why: Audits are a QA activity: they check processes are followed and effective.

whyNot.0: Finding defects in outputs is QC.
whyNot.1: Audits complement testing; outputs still need checking.
whyNot.2: Approval of outputs is acceptance, not an audit's role.

explain.body: QC detects defects and records them. QA looks at the patterns, finds the process causes and improves the process. The result: fewer defects for QC to find next time, and more confidence for the board.

test.q: Which statement BEST describes how QA and QC work together?
options: QC is only needed when QA has failed to prevent defects
QC detects defects; QA uses findings to fix causes
QA is done during planning and QC only after handover
QA and QC are two names for the same set of checks
test.why: QC finds and records defects; QA uses that evidence to improve the processes that cause them.

whyNot.0: QC is always needed: no process prevents every defect.
whyNot.2: QA runs throughout the project, and QC happens as outputs are produced, before handover.
whyNot.3: They are different: QA examines processes, QC examines products.
